Rig-up

Step by step
  1. Select a switch in Rig-up to take an item out or put it back.
  2. Read the Note lines.
  3. Select Restore full rig-up to put all back.
Tips and pitfalls

Tips

  • An item out passes its flow on: H-101 → V-101 → T-201 (or burner, production line) → T-202 / T-301 → P-201 → export. P-201 out: gravity drain; FS-401 out: export line + vent.
  • Optional, out by default: DS-101, T-202, CK-102; also in the toolbar Rig-up menu.
  • V-101 out: no meter rates, GOR (see Appendix B), BS&W (see Appendix B); to T-201 its PCV-201 takes the gas, so gas rates trip PSHH-201 (steady ⚠; FS-5 (see Chapter 12)); no tank in: burner line. Cushion (see Appendix B): FS-1 (see Chapter 12).
  • Saved in project files; the steady check ignores it.

Toolbar and keys

Step by step
  1. 3D / 2D (V). Play / pause (Space). Speed ×1, ×10, ×60, ×600 ([ and ]).
  2. Reset → Reset to steady (R) or Reset → Start from empty (after a minute it asks first): clock, totals and levels clear.
  3. ESD trips SDV-101 (E), after a confirm. Scenarios switches faults (on an item that is out, once it is in) and holds the cushion unload.
  4. 3D only: View (0 to 5), Colour, Labels (L), Quality; tap a CK-101 leg to use it (adjustable: front / right; positive: left / back). Also Legend, Trends, Max (F).
  5. A acknowledges all; ? shows the keys; Esc closes; on a phone, More.

HUD

What it does

T+ clock, speed, RUNNING or PAUSED. WHP, Choke in→out, Sep with its bar (green ±5 psi (34.5 kPa) of set point, amber PAH, red PSHH), Surge. Gas, Oil, Water, GOR (total; 1 · 2 below), BS&W, totals since T+0, tank and alarm lines.

Equipment cards

Step by step
  1. Select equipment in the view: live readings, design values, a trend.
  2. SDV-101 Trip ESD / Reset ESD; CK-101 leg and beans; H-101 Bypass ON; V-101 set point −/+ 5 psi (34.5 kPa).
  3. T-201, T-202: A fills, B transfers, swapped at 80 %; inlets A and B, Auto-divert, valve stroke, LCV suction and trip reset. T-301: inlets, Swap tank. Bean and set point write the form.

DS-101 desander and sand

What it does

Catches sand upstream of the bean, where erosion is worst. Sand: the Dynamic Simulation sand rates or Scenarios → Sand / proppant flow-back (clean-up).

Step by step
  1. Switch Cyclonic desander (upstream of the choke) in, in Rig-up. Its card: ΔP, cut size, capture, accumulator, erosion, rating.
  2. At LAH-103 (80 %) select Dump sand: isolate, bleed, flush (XV-103), equalise, reopen, about 17 minutes; the well flows on.
  3. An ESD holds a dump: after Reset ESD, Resume dump or Abort dump. Auto-dump dumps at its set point.
  4. Bypass (HV-104) sends all the sand to the bean.
Tips and pitfalls

Tips

  • High ΔP: plugged liner (PDAH-103); low: washed out (PDAL-103). A rating below SITHP is ✗.
  • Choke erosion is a screening figure, not a bean life.

T-202 second surge tank

What it does

Like T-201: A | B, inlets XV-202A / B, PCV-203, PCV-204 blanket, PSV-202 (see Appendix B), LCV-202 to T-301 from A, B or A+B (no pump). It starts empty, inlets shut; A fills first.

Step by step
  1. Switch Second surge tank in; open its card.
  2. Route: T-201, T-202 or Both (it opens the T-202 inlet); on Both the lower-pressure tank takes the dumps.
  3. Auto-divert swaps A and B at 80 %; Auto route swaps tanks; after a dry-run trip, Reset LCV-202.
Tips and pitfalls

Tips

  • LSHH-202 shuts the high side only; both shut on T-202 alone: LSHH-102 trips the ESD.

LP flare line and GOR2

What it does

PCV-201 / 203 and PSV-201 / 202 vent via FT-201 to an LP tip on FS-401 (out: vent); T-301 vents unmetered. GOR1 = FE-101 gas ÷ oil, GOR2 = FT-201 gas ÷ oil; the HUD GOR is the total.

CK-102 heater inlet choke

Step by step
  1. Switch Heater inlet choke in, in Rig-up (H-101 must be in).
  2. Set Heater choke CK-102 bean and CK-102 position in the Heater card.
  3. Its card: pressure between the chokes (PAH-102 at 90 % of an assumed 1440 psig (9928 kPa(g)): on from 44/64 down), pair capacity, limiter; exercise 11 (see Chapter 11).

Alarms and ESD

Step by step
  1. The alarm bar shows the newest alarm: Ack.
  2. Alarms: alarms with time and tag, design warnings, Events; Ack all.
  3. After a trip the banner shows the cause; Reset ESD once no trip alarm is active.
Tips and pitfalls

Tips

  • Every trip closes SDV-101 (5 s; 15 s to open, then 180 s grace), except LSHH-301, LSHH-202 and the LCV-201 / LCV-202 low-low.
  • Shut in, WHP builds towards 1.2 × WHP (time constant 300 s).
  • Separator set points follow Operating Pressure: PAH = SP + max(10 %, 15 psi (103 kPa)), PSHH = SP + max(20 %, 25 psi (172 kPa)).

Reports and saving

What it does

Page export and Quick Report: the form, Rig-up card and steady results, not the live view. Inputs autosave; trends keep 4 h. Mini WellOS (see Chapter 6.1) logs the rates.

2D and 3D

What it does

2D: a schematic with live values and a Levels & Pressures strip; select a tank valve to work it.

3D: camera views, Colour overlays (Phase, Pressure, Temperature, Erosion), labels; needs WebGL 2, else 2D with Retry and Use 2D.

Reviewed for v4.1

Well Test Simulator course

1 Normal test: line up, stabilise and read the spread

Goal: Find every reading of a normal test and explain why the choke is in critical flow.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.
  • Select 2D: the clearest view on a projector.

Steps

  1. Check the clock runs (Play) at speed ×10.
  2. Read the HUD: WHP, Choke in→out, Sep, Surge, then Gas, Oil, Water, GOR and BS&W.
  3. Open the CK-101 card: Regime, Downstream P, Capacity, J-T ΔT.
  4. On the V-101 card select + twice next to PCV-101 SP (160 psig (1103 kPa(g))); watch Setpoint ramp.
  5. Follow the trends strip (in 3D: Trends) for 10 minutes of sim time, then set the SP back to 150 psig (1034 kPa(g)).

What to observe

  • Choke outlet about 158 psig (1089 kPa(g)) against 2999 psig (20677 kPa(g)) at the inlet: P2/P1 0.057, far below 0.55: Critical.
  • Capacity 10.71 MMSCFD (303 10³ m³/d) for 10 MMSCFD (283 10³ m³/d) asked: the bean is not limiting.
  • J-T cooling about 111 °F (61.7 °C): choke outlet about 69 °F (20.6 °C), heater outlet 150 °F (65.6 °C).
  • The set point ramps at about 2 psi (13.8 kPa) per second and the separator pressure follows it.

Questions

  • Why does a separator set point of 160 psig (1103 kPa(g)) not change the gas rate?
  • What is the choke ΔP, and where does most of the cooling happen?
  • Which reading warns you that the bean is near its limit?

How the simulator works

A dynamic replay around a steady calculation: wellhead to choke, the choke outlet back-walked from the separator Operating Pressure.

The rates are inputs. The bean is checked against the gas only; too small, and all three rates are cut by the same factor. Form changes apply live and show in Events.

Practise line-ups, levels, alarms, ESD, gauging, upsets, hydrates; it does not predict a well.

On a phone, Reset, Scenarios, Colour, View and Trends are in the More menu.

Using this course with a crew

Self-paced, or run by a trainer (2D on a projector) with the trainer notes and worksheets. Questions: software@h2oil.co.uk.

2 Choke capacity and bean selection

Goal: See what happens when the bean is too small for the gas rate, and size it back.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.

Steps

  1. Select CK-101 in the view to open its card.
  2. Select − once: the bean goes to 30/64.
  3. Open Alarms. Watch CHOKE_LIMIT and the HUD Gas, Oil and Water.
  4. Select − again (28/64) and read Capacity.
  5. Select + until the alarm clears (32/64), then once more (34/64): it stays clear.

What to observe

  • On 30/64 the capacity is 9.41 MMSCFD (266 10³ m³/d): CK-101 raises CHOKE_LIMIT and gas, oil and water are all cut by about 6 %.
  • Capacity follows the bean area: 10.71 × (30/32)² ≈ 9.41.
  • The design warnings in Alarms say “Choke is flow-limited — bean 30/64”.

Questions

  • What capacity do you expect on 28/64?
  • Why does the oil rate fall when only the gas capacity is short?
  • Can this check limit a liquid-only flow?

3 Clean-up: unload the cushion to the burner (V-101 out)

Goal: Unload the completion cushion straight to the burner boom, then go through the separator.

Set-up

  • Base set-up as in exercise 1.

Steps

  1. Follow FS-1 (see Chapter 12): V-101 out to the Burner / flare line, Cushion unload (clean-up) from Scenarios, ×60.
  2. Variant: V-101 in, start the cushion again. Variant 2: Surge tank T-201 (FS-5 (see Chapter 12)).

What to observe

  • WHP rises by itself as the column unloads; the choke outlet stays near 5 psig (34.5 kPa(g)).
  • CUSH_BURNER while cushion liquid goes to the burner.
  • Breakthrough about 41 minutes after the start, then the tail; done after about 3.2 hours with 50 bbl (7.95 m³) recovered.
  • Variant: CUSH_DUMP, LAHH-101 and carry-over within 5 minutes. Variant 2: the water goes on to T-301; PSHH-201 after breakthrough.

Questions

  • Where do the flowing wellhead pressure and the production-line pressure go?
  • Why does WHP rise while the cushion unloads?
  • Why warm the heater before breakthrough?
  • Why does V-101 flood in the variant?

4 Separator upset: dump valve failure

Goal: Recognise a dump valve that does not open, act before the trip, and restart after it.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.

Steps

  1. Run at ×10 for about 10 minutes of sim time.
  2. The trainer sets Scenarios → LCV-102 stuck closed.
  3. Watch the V-101 card: Oil bucket rises, Oil dump stays at 0.
  4. At LAH-102 decide: cut the rate or shut in with ESD before LSHH-102.
  5. After the trip select Reset ESD. It is refused while LSHH-102 is active.
  6. Clear the fault (select it again), wait for the bucket to fall, Ack all, then Reset ESD.

What to observe

  • LAH-102 about 3 minutes after the fault; LSHH-102 trips the ESD less than a minute later.
  • The ESD button tooltip lists the active trips that block the reset.
  • Events records the fault, the alarms, the trip and the reset.

Questions

  • Which reading showed the cause before any alarm?
  • Why is the reset refused?
  • What would a stuck-closed LCV-101 look like?

5 ESD and restart

Goal: Shut in with the ESD, watch the wellhead pressure build and bring the well back.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.

Steps

  1. At steady flow select ESD in the toolbar.
  2. Open the SDV-101 card and watch Travel.
  3. Watch WHP on the HUD for 5 minutes of sim time.
  4. Select Reset ESD.
  5. Watch the flow return and the alarms during the start-up.

What to observe

  • SDV-101 closes in 5 seconds and opens in 15 seconds.
  • WHP builds toward 1.2 × the flowing WHP (time constant 300 seconds): about 3300 psig (22753 kPa(g)) after 5 minutes.
  • After the reset, low alarms are held off for a 180-second start-up grace.

Questions

  • Why does WHP rise after the shut-in?
  • Why are low-pressure and low-level alarms held off after the reset?
  • What do you check before you reopen a real well?

6 Tank gauging and batch rates

Goal: Read a gauge tank batch and compare it with the separator meter.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.

Steps

  1. Run at ×60 for about 2 hours of sim time.
  2. Open the T-301 card. Watch T-301A fill to 90 %, then the inlet change to B.
  3. Watch A go to SETTLING, then DRAINING through P-201.
  4. Read Last batch, BS&W and Shrinkage, and the batch entry in Events.
  5. Variant: the trainer sets Scenarios → P-201 failed (gauge tank pump); run on to LAH-301 and LSHH-301.

What to observe

  • The first batch closes after about 1.1 hours at the default rates and settles for 10 minutes.
  • Gas flashes off in the tanks (shrinkage), but LCV-201 transfers in bursts: a batch can read above the meter.
  • LSHH-301 shuts the LCV-201 transfer but does not trip the ESD.

Questions

  • Why do the tank and the meter disagree?
  • Why wait before you gauge?
  • What happens to the separator when T-301 is full?

7 Surge tank operation

Goal: Run the surge tank transfer, change compartments safely and spot a transfer problem.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.

Steps

  1. Open the T-201 card. Read Level (A+B), Pressure, Transfer and Transfer ΔP.
  2. Under Inlet A fills while LCV-201 draws B down; auto-divert swaps at 80 %. By hand select B, then A at once: A stays open until B is open (open new, then close old).
  3. The trainer sets Scenarios → LCV-201 stuck closed (surge transfer); watch the level and Time to HH.
  4. Clear the fault before LSHH-201, or watch it trip the ESD.
  5. Pause, Surge Tank Pressure 2 psig, Reset → Reset to steady, play, watch Transfer ΔP (lowering it by 23 psi while running trips PSHH-201).

What to observe

  • LCV-201 has no pump: it transfers on the surge tank pressure plus the liquid head.
  • With LCV-201 stuck closed, LSHH-201 trips the ESD about an hour later at the default rates.
  • At 2 psig the transfer ΔP falls to about 1 psi (6.89 kPa) and LCV-201 raises a low ΔP warning.

Questions

  • Why open the new inlet before closing the old one?
  • What drives the transfer to the gauge tank?
  • What would you change for a low-pressure surge tank?

8 Hydrates and the heater

Goal: See where hydrates can form, and what the heater does about it.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.

Steps

  1. In the form set Wellhead Temp to 60 °F (15.6 °C) (live, no Reset).
  2. Watch the choke outlet temperature and the hydrate alarms in Alarms.
  3. Open the H-101 card and select Bypass (ON). See how far the hydrate risk spreads.
  4. Select Bypass again (OFF). Watch the heater outlet warm back up.
  5. In 3D select Colour → Temperature.

What to observe

  • J-T cooling of about 111 °F (61.7 °C) takes the choke outlet to about -51 °F (-46.1 °C); hydrate point about 37 °F (2.78 °C).
  • Even upstream of the choke, 60 °F (15.6 °C) is below the 75 °F (23.9 °C) hydrate point at 3000 psig (20684 kPa(g)).
  • With the heater in, the risk ends at the heater; bypassed, it reaches the separator and the flare line.
  • At 180 °F (82.2 °C) wellhead temperature the outlet is about 69 °F (20.6 °C): about 32 °F (17.8 °C) of margin.

Questions

  • Why is the heater downstream of the choke not enough here?
  • What else could protect the choke?
  • Why does the margin grow as the well warms up?

9 Sand and the desander DS-101

Goal: Catch flow-back sand upstream of the choke, dump the accumulator safely and see what a bypass does to the bean.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.
  • In the Rig-up card switch Cyclonic desander (upstream of the choke) in. DS-101 sits between SDV-101 and CK-101.

Steps

  1. Open the DS-101 card. Read ΔP, Cut size, Capture and Rating.
  2. Start Scenarios → Sand / proppant flow-back (clean-up) and run at ×60. Watch Accumulator and the HUD line DS-101 sand.
  3. At LAH-103 select Dump sand and confirm. Follow Dump: ISOLATING, BLEEDING, FLUSHING, EQUALISING, REOPENING.
  4. After the dump set Bypass ON for 2 minutes and watch To choke and Choke erosion. Then set it OFF.
  5. Variant: select ESD during a dump: it is HELD. After Reset ESD select Resume dump or Abort dump.
  6. Finally switch Cyclonic desander (upstream of the choke) out in Rig-up: Restore full rig-up does not remove it.

What to observe

  • Clean ΔP about 3.9 psi (26.9 kPa), cut size about 40 µm, about 95 % of the formation sand caught; the choke inlet is lower by the ΔP.
  • LAH-103 about 3.5 hours after the flow-back starts, at 80 % of the 663 lb (301 kg) accumulator (about 530 lb (240 kg)).
  • The dump takes about 17 minutes; the well keeps flowing. XV-103 opens below 50 psig (345 kPa(g)) in the accumulator; the isolation reopens within 75 psi (517 kPa) of the desander.
  • Bypassed, all the sand reaches the bean: a CK-101 sand alarm, Choke erosion HIGH. In line again: OK.

Questions

  • Why is the desander upstream of the choke?
  • Why bleed the accumulator before XV-103 opens?
  • What rating does DS-101 need, and why?
  • When may you bypass it?

10 Second surge tank T-202

Goal: Route the separator dumps to the two compartments of T-202 and learn which T-202 trips shut the well in.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.
  • In the Rig-up card switch Second surge tank in. T-202 starts empty, XV-202A / B shut: A to fill, B to transfer.

Steps

  1. Open the T-202 card: level, line-up, T-202A, T-202B, Route, LCV-202.
  2. Under Route select Both. Watch Share of dumps and both tank pressures.
  3. Select T-202: XV-202A opens, then XV-201A closes (open new, then close old). Run at ×60.
  4. The trainer sets Scenarios → LCV-202 stuck closed (T-202 transfer): run to LSHH-202 on T-202 only, then on Both.
  5. Reset, route to T-202 and let the trainer set Scenarios → PCV-203 stuck closed (T-202 back-pressure).
  6. Finally switch Second surge tank out in Rig-up: Restore full rig-up does not remove it.

What to observe

  • At equal pressures the dumps split evenly.
  • T-202 only: A reaches 80 % about 46 minutes after the route; auto-divert to B, LCV-202 empties A to 25 % in about 11 minutes (tank pressure, no pump).
  • LCV-202 stuck, T-202 only: XFER2_FAIL at the divert, LAH-202 both high (about 93 minutes), LSHH-202 shuts B (about 100), then LSHH-102 trips the ESD within a minute. On Both the dumps go on into T-201: no trip.
  • PCV-203 stuck closed: PAH-202 after about 5 minutes; PSHH-202 shuts the inlets and PCV-204 and trips the ESD about 14 minutes after the fault.

Questions

  • Why does the lower-pressure tank take the dumps?
  • Why does LSHH-202 not trip the ESD itself?
  • What protects T-202 from overpressure?

11 Staging the drop with the heater choke CK-102

Goal: Split the pressure drop between CK-101 and CK-102 and find which choke limits the rate.

Set-up

  • Base set-up: Restore full rig-up in the Rig-up card, form defaults, Reset → Reset to steady, then Alarms → Ack all.
  • In the Rig-up card switch Heater inlet choke in (it needs H-101). CK-102 starts on 48/64, On the heater inlet.

Steps

  1. Open the CK-102 card. Read Upstream P (between the chokes), Regime, Pair capacity and Limiter.
  2. Open the CK-101 card and read its regime.
  3. In the form set Heater choke CK-102 bean to 32. Watch the alarms and both cards.
  4. Set it to 64, then back to 48.
  5. On the H-101 card select Bypass: CK-102 goes out of line with it. Select it again.
  6. Finally switch Heater inlet choke out in Rig-up: Restore full rig-up does not remove it.

What to observe

  • On 48/64 about 1135 psig (7826 kPa(g)) between the chokes: CK-101 P2/P1 0.38, Critical, and CK-101 limits the pair (10.71 MMSCFD (303 10³ m³/d)).
  • On 32/64 CK-102 limits: 8.92 MMSCFD (253 10³ m³/d) for 10 MMSCFD (283 10³ m³/d) asked (CHOKE2_LIMIT), CK-101 subcritical (CK1_SUBCRIT); about 2400 psig (16547 kPa(g)) between the chokes at that rate (page and live).
  • On 64/64 about 634 psig (4371 kPa(g)) between the chokes.
  • Expected: the page warns that SITHP (3600 psig (24821 kPa(g)), estimated) is above the assumed 1440 psig (9928 kPa(g)) rating between the chokes; PAH-102 from 44/64 down (1296 psig (8936 kPa(g))).

Questions

  • Why does CK-101 go subcritical on 32/64?
  • Which choke sets the rate on 48/64?
  • What protects the line between the chokes?

Answers

1 Normal test: line up, stabilise and read the spread

  • In critical flow the rate does not depend on the back pressure (P2/P1 stays below about 0.55).
  • About 2842 psi (19595 kPa). Most of the cooling is J-T across the choke.
  • Capacity on the CK-101 card, and the choke capacity bar, against the gas rate.

2 Choke capacity and bean selection

  • 10.71 × (28/32)² ≈ 8.2 MMSCFD (232 10³ m³/d).
  • The model scales the whole stream to the gas capacity.
  • No. The check compares the gas rate only, so the bean never limits a liquid rate.

3 Clean-up: unload the cushion to the burner (V-101 out)

  • FWHP in Wellhead Pressure; line pressure in Production line pressure (V-101 out) or Operating Pressure (V-101 in).
  • The cushion column in the tubing gets shorter, so less of the shut-in pressure is lost to its head.
  • At breakthrough the gas flows again and cools across the choke: a cold heater gives hydrate alarms.
  • Its water dump passes about 790 BPD (126 m³/d), less than the 1500 BPD (238 m³/d) unload rate.

4 Separator upset: dump valve failure

  • Oil dump at 0 while the bucket level rises.
  • A trip alarm is still active; the ESD resets only when every trip has cleared.
  • The interface rises to LAHH-101 and water carries over the weir; it does not trip the ESD.

5 ESD and restart

  • The well keeps feeding the tubing, so pressure builds toward the shut-in pressure.
  • Levels and pressures need time to come back; without the grace they would alarm at every start.
  • The cause is cleared, the line-up is right and the downstream pressure is ready.

6 Tank gauging and batch rates

  • The meter reads live oil at separator conditions; the tank holds stock-tank oil after flash.
  • Gas and water need time to separate before a dip or a strap is taken.
  • LCV-201 stops; the surge tank then fills, so watch its level.

7 Surge tank operation

  • So the separator dumps are never blocked during the change.
  • The surge tank pressure and the liquid head, against the lift to the gauge tank inlet.
  • Keep enough pressure for the lift, or plan for a slower transfer.

8 Hydrates and the heater

  • The coldest point is the choke outlet, before the heater.
  • Inhibitor injection upstream of the choke: see Hydrate Management (see Chapter 7.3) and Chemical Injection (see Chapter 7.4).
  • A hotter stream leaves the choke above the hydrate point.

9 Sand and the desander DS-101

  • Sand erodes the bean fastest (highest velocity); catching it upstream protects it.
  • XV-103 dumps to an open skip: at wellhead pressure the sand and gas would blow out.
  • At least the maximum shut-in WHP: SDV-101 is its only shut-in and it has no relief valve; PSHH-103 trips the ESD at the rating.
  • For maintenance, or once the well is sand-free.

10 Second surge tank T-202

  • Each branch is check-valved into its own gas space: liquid goes only where the header is above the tank pressure.
  • Shutting the inlet protects the tank; the well is shut in only if the dumps then have nowhere to go.
  • PCV-203, then PSHH-202 (inlets and the blanket PCV-204 shut, then ESD), then PSV-202.

11 Staging the drop with the heater choke CK-102

  • CK-102 holds the pressure between the chokes above about 0.55 of the CK-101 inlet.
  • CK-101: it is still critical and the pair passes its capacity.
  • Its design pressure, PAH-102 at 90 % and the blocked-in check; no relief valve is modelled between the chokes.

Trainer notes

1 Normal test: line up, stabilise and read the spread

Duration: 20–30 minutes.

Fault to inject: None. Ask the crew to call out each reading as on a real job.

A good response: Reads WHP, choke in and out, separator pressure against SP, levels and rates unaided; explains critical flow.

Common mistakes:

  • Expecting the rate to change with the separator pressure.
  • Taking the choke upstream pressure for the wellhead pressure.

Debrief questions:

  • What would make this choke go subcritical?
  • Which readings would you log every 15 minutes?
  • Where would you look first if GOR jumped?

2 Choke capacity and bean selection

Duration: 15–20 minutes.

Fault to inject: Variant: set Adjustable choke bean to 28 beforehand; the trainee finds CHOKE_LIMIT and diagnoses it.

A good response: Reads Capacity against the gas rate and clears the alarm with the smallest bean that passes it.

Common mistakes:

  • Raising the bean far past the need.
  • Thinking the liquid rate sets the bean.

Debrief questions:

  • How do you size a bean before the test?
  • What does a flow-limited choke do to the test data?
  • What else changes on a larger bean?

3 Clean-up: unload the cushion to the burner (V-101 out)

Duration: 30–40 minutes.

Fault to inject: None at first. Variant: bean 12/64 and a low gas rate, and let the trainee find CUSH_LIMIT.

A good response: Sets the destination first, warns the burner crew (CUSH_BURNER), warms the heater before breakthrough, goes through V-101 only on clean returns.

Common mistakes:

  • Putting the production or flowing pressure in Operating Pressure.
  • Unloading through V-101 faster than its water dump.
  • Sending an oil or diesel cushion to the burner without a plan.

Debrief questions:

  • What is the real back pressure of your burner line?
  • What tells you the cushion is out?
  • When is it time to go through the separator?

4 Separator upset: dump valve failure

Duration: 20 minutes.

Fault to inject: At about 10 minutes of sim time: Scenarios → LCV-102 stuck closed, with the projector blanked.

A good response: Spots Oil dump at 0, names LCV-102, shuts in under control and resets in the right order.

Common mistakes:

  • Acknowledging alarms without reading them.
  • Trying Reset ESD again and again.

Debrief questions:

  • What would you check on a real LCV-102?
  • How long did you have between LAH and LSHH?
  • What does a trip cost the test?

5 ESD and restart

Duration: 15 minutes.

Fault to inject: None, or trip the ESD yourself at an unexpected time and ask for the restart.

A good response: Confirms SDV-101 is shut, logs the shut-in pressure and restarts in order.

Common mistakes:

  • Resetting before reading the cause in Events.
  • Expecting full flow at once after the reset.

Debrief questions:

  • What would the build-up tell a reservoir engineer?
  • Which trips should never be reset from the panel?
  • What is the order of a restart on your spread?

6 Tank gauging and batch rates

Duration: 30 minutes.

Fault to inject: Variant: after the first batch, Scenarios → P-201 failed (gauge tank pump).

A good response: Reads the batch and explains shrinkage; with P-201 failed, plans the next tank before LSHH-301.

Common mistakes:

  • Gauging a tank that is still settling.
  • Reporting the meter rate as the tank rate.

Debrief questions:

  • How do you correct a tank batch to standard conditions?
  • What makes the meter factor drift?
  • What do you do with no pump?

7 Surge tank operation

Duration: 25 minutes.

Fault to inject: At about 10 minutes of sim time: Scenarios → LCV-201 stuck closed (surge transfer).

A good response: Reads Time to HH, reacts before LSHH-201 and changes compartments in the right order.

Common mistakes:

  • Shutting both inlets.
  • Ignoring the low ΔP warning.

Debrief questions:

  • What protects the surge tank from overpressure?
  • How long can you run with no transfer?
  • Where does the flash gas go?

8 Hydrates and the heater

Duration: 20 minutes.

Fault to inject: None. Variant: start with the heater bypassed and ask for a safe start-up plan.

A good response: Finds the coldest point, puts the heater in and asks for inhibitor at the choke.

Common mistakes:

  • Looking only at the separator temperature.
  • Bypassing the heater to save fuel on a cold well.

Debrief questions:

  • Where would you inject inhibitor on your spread?
  • How does the choke outlet temperature change with the bean?
  • What is your hydrate margin rule?

9 Sand and the desander DS-101

Duration: 30–40 minutes.

Fault to inject: After the first dump: Scenarios → XV-103 stuck closed (desander dump), then ask for another dump.

A good response: Dumps at LAH-103, reads the dump-fail alarm and does not bypass to get rid of it.

Common mistakes:

  • Bypassing DS-101 during the flow-back.
  • Expecting a shut-in for every dump.

Debrief questions:

  • How would you spot a washed-out liner?
  • What would a passing upper isolation do to the dump?
  • How often would you dump on this well?

10 Second surge tank T-202

Duration: 30 minutes.

Fault to inject: At about 10 minutes on T-202 only: Scenarios → LCV-202 stuck closed (T-202 transfer).

A good response: Watches Time to HH, routes to Both or T-201 before LSHH-202 and keeps the dumps open.

Common mistakes:

  • Routing to T-202 only and walking away.
  • Shutting every inlet.

Debrief questions:

  • When would you run two surge tanks?
  • What does a blocked back-pressure valve look like?
  • Why keep separate gas spaces?

11 Staging the drop with the heater choke CK-102

Duration: 20 minutes.

Fault to inject: None. Variant: start on 32/64 and ask why the rate is short.

A good response: Reads the pressure between the chokes and the limiter, and opens CK-102 until CK-101 is critical again.

Common mistakes:

  • Pinching CK-102 below the CK-101 bean.
  • Forgetting that the heater bypass takes CK-102 out of line.

Debrief questions:

  • Where would a second choke sit on your spread?
  • Why stage the drop?
  • What if CK-102 plugged with hydrate?

12 Field scenarios

FS-1 Unloading the completion cushion straight to the burner boom

Which pressure goes where

Well testers use “production pressure” for two different things, so check which one you have.

The pressure you haveWhere it goesRig-upScenario
Flowing wellhead or tubing pressure (FWHP, FTHP, flowing pressure)Wellhead Pressure, never the separator pressureanyall
Production or export line pressure (the header the well flows into)V-101 in: Operating Pressure plus the line loss. V-101 out: Production line pressure, destination Production lineV-101 in or outFS-2 (see Chapter 12)
Burner boom (cushion or clean-up straight to the burner)Nothing to enter: destination Burner / flare line (5 psig (34.5 kPa(g)) header)V-101 outFS-1 (see Chapter 12)
Flow-back to the tanksDestination Surge tank T-201, at Surge Tank PressureV-101 outFS-5 (see Chapter 12)
Surge tank back pressureSurge Tank Pressure, at most 30 psig; 10 psi below Operating Pressure with V-101 inanyall
What Operating Pressure controlsV-101 inV-101 out
Live model: PCV-101 set point and separator pressureyesno (PCV-101 held shut)
Live model: separator alarms and relief (PAH, PSHH, PAL, PSV)set from itlive on the trapped vessel: lowering it trips PSHH-101
Choke outlet: steady check and live modelseparator pressure + line lossesno: the destination pressure + the whole-stream line loss
Surge Tank Pressure limit (Operating Pressure − 10 psi)yesno (at most 30 psig only)
  1. In Dynamic Simulation set With V-101 out, well stream to → Burner / flare line; switch V-101 (Test separator) out. Leave Operating and Surge Tank Pressure.
  2. Form: the flowing WHP in Wellhead Pressure, the expected rates. Keep H-101 in and warm.
  3. Scenarios, Cushion unload (clean-up): Cushion volume, Cushion SG, Unload rate, Tubing, Tubing depth (50 bbl (7.95 m³), SG 1.03, 1500 BPD (238 m³/d), 3-1/2″ to 10000 ft (3048 m)), Start.
  4. Run at ×60. The WHP target drops to about 1700 psig (11721 kPa(g)) (the gauge bottoms near 1840 psig (12686 kPa(g)) after about 3 minutes) and rises as the column unloads; the choke outlet stays near 5 psig (34.5 kPa(g)).
  5. CUSH_BURNER: cushion liquid at the burner (water or brine: flame-out; oil or diesel: burning fallout).
  6. Breakthrough about 41 minutes after the start: gas returns, WHP peaks near 3460 psig (23856 kPa(g)), then settles while the tail comes out. Done after about 3.2 hours, 50 bbl (7.95 m³) recovered.
  7. At the full gas rate the choke outlet rises to about 35 psig (241 kPa(g)) and the velocity alarms (Choke→Heater, Heater→Sep, Sep→Flare) show the burner line is too small: cut the bean, or go through the separator once returns are clean.

The bean can limit the liquid: CUSH_LIMIT (12/64 at 1 MMSCFD (28.3 10³ m³/d): about 1200 BPD (191 m³/d)). A well that cannot lift the cushion: CUSH_NOLIFT. H-101 at its limit: HTR_FULL.

Through V-101 the water dump passes about 790 BPD (126 m³/d): Start warns, CUSH_DUMP stays up, LAHH-101 within 5 minutes.

Limits

Liquid orifice law for the bean; flare-line geometry, no riser for the line loss; burning liquid is warned about only.

FS-2 Flowing straight to a production line

Which pressure goes where

The flowing WHP goes in Wellhead Pressure; the production-line pressure in Operating Pressure with V-101 in.

The pressure you haveWhere it goesRig-upScenario
Flowing wellhead or tubing pressure (FWHP, FTHP, flowing pressure)Wellhead Pressure, never the separator pressureanyall
Production or export line pressure (the header the well flows into)V-101 in: Operating Pressure plus the line loss. V-101 out: Production line pressure, destination Production lineV-101 in or outFS-2 (see Chapter 12)
Burner boom (cushion or clean-up straight to the burner)Nothing to enter: destination Burner / flare line (5 psig (34.5 kPa(g)) header)V-101 outFS-1 (see Chapter 12)
Flow-back to the tanksDestination Surge tank T-201, at Surge Tank PressureV-101 outFS-5 (see Chapter 12)
Surge tank back pressureSurge Tank Pressure, at most 30 psig; 10 psi below Operating Pressure with V-101 inanyall
  1. In Dynamic Simulation: With V-101 out, well stream to → Production line, Production line pressure = the tie-in pressure (0 to 1440 psig).
  2. Rig-up: switch V-101 out. FS-401 may be out too: tank relief then goes to vent (HUD To vent).
  3. At 300 psig the choke outlet is about 308 psig (2124 kPa(g)), P2/P1 0.107, Critical; totals in To production line.
  4. Tie-in NRV-501 / XV-501; shut in, NRV-501 holds the spread at line pressure. PSHH-104 (H-101 outlet) trips SDV-101 at 90 % of the 1440 psig (9928 kPa(g)) bypass-path rating: a line above about 1290 psig shuts the well in (the page warns), the ESD resets only below it. SEPBY_RATING: choke outlet above the rating.
  5. A line pressure near the choke inlet makes CK-101 subcritical (WHP 1000 psig (6895 kPa(g)) into 600 psig: P2/P1 0.61); a real rate would then follow the line.

What it gets wrong

  • The line pressure is constant; a real header varies.
  • No blocked-outlet dynamics.
  • No metering by design: V-101 is out.

FS-3 Clean-up with sand: the desander upstream of the choke

A clean-up after a frac or gravel pack brings back proppant; DS-101 catches it upstream of the choke (exercise 9 (see Chapter 11)).

  1. Rig-up: switch Cyclonic desander (upstream of the choke) in; keep your clean-up line-up (through V-101, or to the burner as in FS-1 (see Chapter 12)).
  2. Rating: set Desander rating (psi) and Max shut-in wellhead pressure (psig) (blank: 1.2 × WHP, 3600 psig here). A rating below it is ✗ on the DS-101 card: no relief valve, not fit for this well.
  3. Sand (imperial-only inputs): set Sand rate, liquid (lb/1000 bbl) and Sand median size (µm), or start Scenarios → Sand / proppant flow-back (clean-up) (LAH-103 about 3.5 hours later).
  4. Dump at LAH-103 (Dump sand, about 17 minutes; the well keeps flowing). Rising ΔP: plugged liner or packed accumulator (PDAH-103). Low ΔP: washed-out liner (PDAL-103).
  5. Keep DS-101 in line while sand comes back: at 10 lb per 1,000 bbl it cuts the choke erosion rate about 68 times (WARN without, OK with).

Limits

Choke erosion is a steel-equivalent screening figure for comparing cases. Sand at V-101 is counted, not settled. The steady check leaves out the desander ΔP.

FS-4 Cold start-up and hydrates

A shut-in well arrives cold and J-T cooling takes the choke outlet far below the hydrate point: plan heater and inhibitor first.

  1. Start with Wellhead Temp 60 °F (15.6 °C) and heater Bypass “Yes — Full Bypass” (heater not lit).
  2. The steady check shows hydrate risk from the wellhead to the flare line: choke outlet about -51 °F (-46.1 °C), hydrate point about 37 °F (2.78 °C).
  3. Put the heater in (Bypass No): the risk clears downstream of it, but WH→ESD, ESD→Choke and Choke→Heater still warn.
  4. Protect the choke with inhibitor upstream of it: work out the margin on Hydrate Management (see Chapter 7.3) and the injection rate on Chemical Injection (see Chapter 7.4).
  5. As the well warms to 180 °F (82.2 °C), the choke outlet rises to about 69 °F (20.6 °C) and the warnings clear.

The H-101 card shows the heater warming up over minutes (exercise 8 (see Chapter 11)).

Staging with CK-102

Switch Heater inlet choke in; pinch CK-102 as you open CK-101 so each takes part of the drop, both outlets 10 °F (5.56 °C) above the hydrate point (CK-102 card Hydrate T / margin). Between the coil passes heats before the second drop. Between the chokes (1440 psig (9928 kPa(g))): PAH-102, blocked-in warning (exercise 11 (see Chapter 11)).

Limits

The simulator raises hydrate alarms; it does not model a hydrate plug building up or the inhibitor itself.

FS-5 Clean-up to the tanks: V-101 out to the surge tank

A low-gas clean-up can skip the separator: T-201 takes the whole stream, PCV-201 vents its gas to the LP flare line, LCV-201 sends the liquid on to T-301.

  1. In Dynamic Simulation keep the V-101-out destination Surge tank T-201. Set Gas Rate to 1 MMSCFD (28.3 10³ m³/d).
  2. Start Cushion unload (clean-up) from Scenarios, then at once switch V-101 (Test separator) out: the column holds the gas back (before the start PSHH-201 trips in seconds).
  3. SEPBY_SURGE_CAP: PCV-201 takes about 0.15 MMSCFD (4.25 10³ m³/d) below PSHH-201; the steady result warns: PSHH-201 TRIP. At ×60 about 26 bbl (4.13 m³) of water reaches T-301 by breakthrough.
  4. Breakthrough after about 41 minutes: the gas returns at the well rate, PAH-201, then PSHH-201 shuts the well in 4 minutes later, unless V-101 went back in first.

Limits

PCV-201 is not resized; no foam or slugs.

Appendix B Glossary

after-closure
The falloff after closure: reservoir flow, for p_i and k.
bean
A fixed choke. Its size is the bore in 64ths of an inch: a 32 bean is 32/64 in.
BS&W
Basic sediment and water: the water and solids in the oil, in % of volume.
closure
The pressure at which the fracture closes: the minimum stress.
critical (sonic) flow
Flow through a choke at sonic speed, below a P2/P1 of about 0.55. The rate then does not depend on the downstream pressure.
cushion
A liquid column (water, brine or diesel) or nitrogen placed in the test string above the tester valve. It limits the drawdown and the collapse load when the valve opens. It is unloaded first, usually to the burner.
DFIT
Diagnostic fracture injection test: a small injection that opens a fracture, then a falloff.
families
Closure methods grouped by what they read, F0 to F4; one vote each.
fluid efficiency
Fracture volume over injected volume at shut-in (η).
FWHP
Flowing wellhead (tubing) pressure, upstream of the choke.
G-function
Dimensionless shut-in time for closure plots.
GOR
Gas-oil ratio: standard gas volume per stock-tank barrel of oil.
height recession
The fracture closes on higher-stress layers first.
IARF
Infinite-acting radial flow: the flat part of the derivative. Permeability and skin come from it.
impulse
After-closure lines that treat the injection as a pulse.
ISIP
Instantaneous shut-in pressure, without friction.
net pressure
ISIP minus closure.
PDL
Pressure-dependent leak-off: fissures open above their stress.
p*
The pressure the semilog straight line of a build-up reaches at infinite shut-in time (Horner time ratio of 1).
PSV
Pressure safety (relief) valve: opens at its set pressure to protect a vessel or line.
R_vis
Closure visibility: the fracture share of the storage.
SITHP
Shut-in tubing (wellhead) pressure with the well closed in.
skin
A dimensionless number for the extra pressure drop near the wellbore. Positive: damage. Negative: a stimulated well.
tip extension
The fracture grows after shut-in.

Appendix D Troubleshooting and FAQ

Which pressure goes where in the Well Test Simulator?

  • Flowing wellhead or tubing pressure: Wellhead Pressure, never the separator pressure.
  • Production or export line pressure: with V-101 in, the separator Operating Pressure plus the line loss to the header; with V-101 out, Production line pressure (FS-2 (see Chapter 12)).
  • Cushion or clean-up straight to the burner: V-101 out to the Burner / flare line, then the cushion scenario (FS-1 (see Chapter 12)).

The steps are in FS-1, FS-2 and the Well Test Simulator (see Chapter 11.1) guide.

Is there training for the simulator?

Help has a self-paced Well Test Simulator course (see Chapter 11). Each exercise has answers, trainer notes and a worksheet, so a supervisor can run it for a crew.

Questions about training: software@h2oil.co.uk.

Can the simulator train sand handling and a second surge tank?

Yes. Switch the optional DS-101 desander and T-202 second surge tank in, in the Rig-up card (Well Test Simulator (see Chapter 11.1)), then follow exercise 9 (see Chapter 11), exercise 10 (see Chapter 11) and field scenario FS-3 (see Chapter 12).

Why is the DFIT closure a range, and the label uncalibrated?

Methods read different events and can disagree a lot; PRiSM then carries both ends. Labels are provisional rules, not yet calibrated.

Is my work saved?

Yes, on this device, as you type. To keep a copy or move it, save a project file (Saving work (see Chapter 1)).

How do I move my work to another device?

File → Save on the first device, then File → Open… on the other one.

Why does a value change when I select Metric?

It is the same value converted. Calculations always run in oilfield units (Units (see Chapter 1)).

Why is the client name missing from my report?

Select Save Information in Client & Well Info (see Chapter 2.3): reports use the saved details.

Does the app work offline?

Yes. The web version works offline after the first visit; the iOS app always does. A few optional parts download a code library the first time they are used.

How do I start again?

Save a project file, then File → New. A new well also starts with empty pages.

Who do I contact?

software@h2oil.co.uk. Please quote the version shown under the logo.
